questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I have a personal connection to Japan with friends in the north of the country. Therefore, Japan was an attractive destination to me. I had been there on multiple occasions and the possibility to live a few months in Tokyo was an exciting prospect.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The Graduate School of Frontier sciences was very forthcoming with administrative help, yet finding relevant information was a bit like pulling teeth. Finding out how and when to register for classes was difficult and some of the info i received was misleading and led me to not be able to attend a course that I was excited about. That was frustrating.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Supervision, help with housing (did not take up this offer), administrative assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It is definitely more expensive but has the advantage that you can live I an area that suits you. You also most likely need to get special monthly apartments; most normal rental contracts are long term and private landlords at large prefer Japanese tenants. Here are some websites:
https://www.unionmonthly.jp/english/
https://atinn.jp/en

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It can be lonely if you live away from others, so you need to very actively engage in international groups and try to make friends during your classes.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I can't say

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was messy. For a long time I was not sure what courses would actually be offered. The curriculum is only finalized rather late after I had applied for pre-approval. Luckily the curriculum of the previous year (the one found online) is quite accurate, but it added an unnecessary level of stress at the time not knowing if I would actually be able to take the courses. The registration is also overly complicated. As an exchange student I needed to hand in a physical course registration sheet with along with a physical approval of my supervisor. Then I was unable to take one of the courses I was officially registered for since there was a separate selection procedure internal to the course. This was frustrating, since the administrative office in my graduate school had told me I had to do nothing else if I was registered. I had to once again get a physical approval from my supervisor for a different course etc. etc. Moreover, there is a lack of understanding at many levels when it comes to exchange students, especially when you take courses at multiple graduate schools. Everyone seems to think that different rules and procedures apply.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Administrative help and help from the supervisor.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Mostly successful but the situation explained above was annoying.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Get in touch with the professors or teaching assistants of courses you want to take and inform them of your interest in the class and ask them whether there are any special requirements or procedures you should be aware of.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It varied very widely; some were extremely easy and basically free credits, others were quite tough and yet others again were easy but required far too much boring work.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Varies on the graduate school and the teachers. The better ones are extremely interactive and practical, and that in the political sciences. The more basic courses are about the same as in CPH, with one very important difference. The hours per class are a lot less, only 1:45 per week per class or so, so courses cannot go into depth on one subject. This is silly.

questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Graduate School of Public Policy / 5130076 International Organizations for Sustainable Development
Great course. Every week you get speakers from different IOs, so you get real insights into the work in these organizations. The speakers change from year to year. This is followed by student discussions and then a Q&A. From a Climate Change standpoint maybe not always super relevant, but extremely interesting and engaging. 


Graduate School of Public Policy / 5123485 Environmental Economics 
Very tough course that could be taught better, but interesting and engaging. I do not agree with many of the concepts that were being taught, but it is good an important to understand how environmental economics functions. Don't come here for a critical approach to EE.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be prepared for an administrative mess and be proactive in getting in touch with profs whose classes you want to take.
2. Reach out to internationals via available forums (we had a Whatsapp group) and make sure to join events. You will find your people quickly.
3. Take a few interesting classes but try to take most with little coursework if possible. You want to be able to enjoy your time and not be stuck summarizing academic papers each week just for the purpose of summarizing academic papers.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not as of now.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new people. Living in an amazing city. Winter in the north.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Managing the bureaucracy of Uni and municipality, especially with language barriers. I was pretty sick in the beginning and needed antibiotics, all while being stuck in a tiny apartment by myself.
